items.title: L9: When a minister rejects your advice
items.source: Civil Service Code; Managing Public Money; Cabinet Manual
items.body: Officials advise and ministers decide. The Civil Service Code requires officials to give honest, objective advice, and then to carry out lawful decisions loyally, even if the minister has chosen a different option. This is not the same as silence. Before the decision, officials should make sure the minister understands the risks, the evidence and the realistic alternatives, and that the advice is recorded. After the decision, officials implement it and do not undermine it by obstruction, delay or briefing against it. There are limits. If the instruction is unlawful, officials must not carry it out and should say so, taking legal advice. If it would breach the Civil Service Code, for example by requiring them to mislead Parliament, they should raise it through the Code's routes. If the decision involves spending that the accounting officer believes fails the tests of regularity, propriety, value for money or feasibility, the accounting officer can ask for a written ministerial direction; for feasibility concerns the issue is whether the plan can be delivered, which is often where officials and ministers differ. A decision that is merely unwise or politically risky is for the minister, who is accountable to Parliament and the electorate. Officials should keep their professional judgement independent of what is popular, but accept that the choice of policy is not theirs. A useful test is whether the issue is about the merits, which belong to ministers, or about legality, propriety, and honesty, which officials cannot set aside. Recording the advice protects both sides, because it shows what the minister knew when deciding. Officials can also make sure the minister has a chance to reconsider if new evidence emerges.

questions.prompt: A minister chooses an option you advised against. It is lawful, affordable and within the department's powers. What best describes your duty?

options.text: Implement it, but slowly, so the minister has time to reconsider before any money is committed
Implement it loyally, having ensured the advice and decision are recorded
Implement it, but tell stakeholders that officials had preferred a different option
Decline to implement it, since officials' professional judgement should prevail on merits

questions.hint: Merits belong to ministers; legality and honesty do not.

questions.prompt: Which concern would justify a ministerial direction rather than simply recording disagreement?

options.text: The accounting officer believes the spending fails the value for money test
An official thinks the policy will be unpopular with the public and the press
A press officer fears the announcement will attract criticism from commentators
A special adviser dislikes the wording of the minister's proposed statement

questions.hint: Directions relate to the accounting officer's four standards.

questions.prompt: After a decision, a team member leaks that officials had warned against it. Which is the best description?

options.text: It is acceptable, because the public has a right to know what advice ministers rejected
It is acceptable, provided the minister is not named in the story that follows
It is acceptable, since the advice itself was honest and accurate
It undermines impartiality and confidentiality, and is no proper way to disagree

questions.hint: Disagreement is expressed through advice, not leaks.

questions.prompt: A minister asks officials to present only the evidence supporting their preferred option. What does the Code require?

options.text: Present only the supporting evidence, because the minister is entitled to decide the framing
Present both sides, but place the inconvenient evidence in a footnote at the end
Present the facts and options accurately, including inconvenient evidence
Present the supporting evidence and offer the rest only if the minister asks for it

questions.hint: Objectivity means not ignoring inconvenient facts.

questions.prompt: What is the main value of recording the advice given to a minister?

options.text: It lets officials claim credit later if the minister's decision turns out well
It gives the opposition material to use if the minister's decision turns out badly
It shows what the minister knew when deciding and protects both sides
It lets the Treasury veto the policy if it disagrees with the department's advice

questions.prompt: A minister's decision is lawful but, in your view, politically damaging. Which action is proper?

options.text: Make sure they understand the risk, then implement the decision
Delay the work until after the next news cycle, in the hope that the minister changes course
Ask the Prime Minister's office to intervene and overrule the minister
Ask the Civil Service Commission for a ruling on whether the decision is wise

questions.hint: Political risk is for the minister.

questions.prompt: A minister instructs officials to do something which they believe would be unlawful. What should they do?

options.text: Proceed, since the minister, not the official, takes responsibility for the decision
Proceed, but put their disagreement in writing in a note to the file
Proceed in a reduced form, so as to limit the legal risk to the department
Say so, seek legal advice and not proceed until the position is clear

questions.hint: Officials cannot carry out unlawful instructions.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a legitimate way to give a minister the chance to reconsider?

options.text: Brief journalists about the new evidence so the pressure for change comes from outside
Submit new evidence with a short note explaining why it may change the advice
Withhold the policy work until the minister agrees to change the decision
Copy the paper to the opposition so they can raise the new evidence

questions.hint: Reconsideration should be through proper advice.

items.title: L9: Who answers when an agency fails
items.source: Cabinet Manual; Cabinet Office, Ministerial responsibility and accountability; Managing Public Money
items.body: When a public service fails, the question 'who is responsible?' is not simple. Ministers are accountable to Parliament for the policy and for the overall framework of an agency or arm's length body. The chief executive of an executive agency is accountable to the minister and, as accounting officer, to Parliament for the agency's use of resources and its operational delivery. The permanent secretary of the parent department is responsible for assurance that the agency is well run. Officials in the sponsor team monitor performance. The distinction between policy and operations is useful but not clean. A minister is expected to answer to Parliament even for operational failures, although they need not take personal blame for what they did not know or authorise. Traditionally, resignation for a department's failure was expected only if the minister was personally culpable or had given misleading information. The Crichel Down case in the 1950s, in which civil servants made mistakes without the minister's knowledge, is often cited as the origin of modern ideas, but practice has varied. Today, the guidance emphasises that ministers are accountable for explaining what has gone wrong and what is being done to put it right, while officials are accountable for explaining their own actions and carrying out their responsibilities properly. A framework document may clarify who is responsible for which decisions, but it does not remove ministerial accountability to Parliament. Where the failure was caused by a policy decision, the minister is more directly answerable. Where it was caused by poor management, the chief executive and the accounting officer may be called by the Public Accounts Committee. Accountability should be explained clearly to Parliament and the public, without evasion, and the aim should be to learn.

questions.prompt: A failure in an agency's IT system causes thousands of delayed payments. Which accounts for the minister's responsibility?

options.text: They are responsible only for policy, so Parliament cannot ask them about an operational failure
They must explain what went wrong and what is being done, even though operations are delegated
They must resign in every case where a delivery body fails
They are responsible only if they personally ordered the system that failed

questions.hint: Ministers answer to Parliament for their department's failures.

questions.prompt: A chief executive believes the failure arose because the department imposed an unrealistic deadline in policy. How is accountability best shown?

options.text: The chief executive alone is accountable, because the failure arose in operations
The permanent secretary alone is accountable, as the most senior official in the department
The minister for the policy choice, the chief executive for managing delivery
Nobody can be held accountable, because the cause is shared between policy and delivery

questions.hint: Accountability depends on the source of failure.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the Crichel Down case is most accurate?

options.text: It established that ministers must always resign when a department fails
It created the Civil Service Code that now governs officials' conduct
It established that agencies are independent of ministers in operational matters
It is often cited when discussing ministers' responsibility for officials' errors

questions.hint: It is a reference point, not a fixed rule.

questions.prompt: What does a framework document do about accountability?

options.text: It clarifies roles, but does not remove ministerial accountability to Parliament
It transfers all responsibility for failures to the agency's chief executive
It prevents Parliament from questioning the agency's chief executive or board
It sets out the penalties that ministers must apply when delivery fails

questions.prompt: The Public Accounts Committee wants an explanation for poor management of a contract at an agency. Whom is it most likely to call?

options.text: The Prime Minister, since the agency's work is the responsibility of the whole government
The agency's chief executive and the department's permanent secretary
The Cabinet Secretary, as head of the Civil Service and all agencies
The Speaker of the House, who supervises Parliament's questioning of agencies

questions.prompt: A minister gives Parliament a clear and honest account of a failure and a credible plan to fix it. How does this relate to resignation?

options.text: It is required for every failure in a department, however the failure arose
It is never expected of a minister, whatever the circumstances of the failure
It is traditionally expected where a minister was personally culpable or misled Parliament
It is decided by the Civil Service Commission after an inquiry under the Code

questions.hint: Practice has been about culpability and honesty.

questions.prompt: What should officials do when asked to explain their own part in a failure?

options.text: Defend the minister's decisions as if they were their own
Say that the failure was the supplier's fault, whatever the facts show
Decline to answer on grounds that advice to ministers is confidential
Account for their own actions honestly and leave policy choices to the minister

questions.hint: Officials account for their own responsibilities.

questions.prompt: What is the main aim of explaining accountability after a failure?

options.text: To be clear and open and to learn, not to evade or find a scapegoat
To spread responsibility so widely that no individual is blamed
To protect the department's reputation by controlling the account given
To limit the information available to Parliament while the review continues

items.title: L9: Transparency versus a safe space
items.source: Freedom of Information Act 2000, s35 and s36; ICO guidance on policy formulation
items.body: Government needs both openness and the ability to deliberate in private. Open government lets the public see how decisions are made and scrutinise them. Private discussion helps officials and ministers weigh options frankly, without fear that half-formed ideas will be reported as policy. The Freedom of Information Act tries to balance these through exemptions that depend on the public interest. Section 35 covers the formulation of government policy and ministerial communications, and section 36 covers information whose disclosure would, in the reasonable opinion of a qualified person, prejudice the effective conduct of public affairs, for instance by inhibiting free and frank advice. Both are qualified exemptions, so the public interest test applies. The ICO accepts that there is a public interest in a safe space to develop policy while it is live, and in avoiding the chilling effect of disclosure on candid advice. But those arguments carry less weight when the policy has been decided, and carry less weight against strong public interest in transparency, for example where there is evidence of wrongdoing, a significant public debate, or large sums of money. A decision to withhold must be specific to the content, not a blanket refusal because information is about policy. Officials also have to balance candour in writing against the risk of disclosure. The right response is not to avoid writing things down, because the Code requires accurate records, but to write professionally and factually. Choosing not to record a decision to avoid disclosure would be improper. Officials should present both sides of the public interest honestly to the decision-maker and not simply argue for withholding.

questions.prompt: A request seeks policy advice on a decision that was announced and implemented last year. How does the passage of time affect the safe space argument?

options.text: It carries more weight, because the advice has become part of the historic record
It no longer matters, because the exemption expires when a decision is announced
It is unaffected, because the principle applies to policy advice at any time
It carries less weight, because the policy is no longer being developed

questions.hint: Safe space strongest while policy is live.

questions.prompt: An official proposes to stop recording meetings so that nothing can be requested. What is the right assessment?

options.text: Improper, because accurate records are required whatever disclosure may follow
Sensible, if limited to the most sensitive meetings, since the safe space matters
Acceptable if the minister agrees to the practice
Required, since the safe space principle obliges officials to avoid creating records

questions.prompt: What does the 'qualified person' do under section 36?

options.text: Decides the public interest test on behalf of the Information Commissioner in each case
Represents the person who made the request during the department's internal review
Gives a reasonable opinion that disclosure would prejudice effective conduct of public affairs
Audits the department's FOI performance on behalf of the Information Commissioner

questions.hint: Section 36 relies on an authorised person's opinion.

questions.prompt: Which factor would strengthen the public interest in disclosure of policy advice?

options.text: The advice was written by senior officials, which makes it more valuable to publish
Evidence of wrongdoing or a significant public debate about large sums of public money
Journalists would like to report the advice, which in itself shows public interest
The advice is classified Official, so releasing it is already thought low risk

questions.hint: Strong transparency interests can outweigh safe space.

questions.prompt: A decision-maker asks for a recommendation on withholding. How should the FOI officer present it?

options.text: Give only the arguments for withholding, to protect the department from criticism
Set out the arguments on both sides of the public interest honestly
Give only the arguments for disclosure, so that the department appears open
Give no arguments, just the outcome the department would prefer

questions.prompt: Which approach to a policy-related request is wrong?

options.text: Withholding all policy information because it is about policy
Considering what the specific information would reveal and how sensitive it is
Disclosing factual material that does not reveal the substance of any advice
Considering whether the decision has now been taken or is still under discussion

questions.hint: A blanket refusal ignores the test.

questions.prompt: What is the 'chilling effect' argument?

options.text: That releasing information makes offices colder, with less opportunity for informal talks
That requests slow down the department and make it less efficient
That disclosure might make officials less willing to give candid advice
That FOI does not cover advice, so officials write less down

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly reflects the Code's honesty value in this context?

options.text: Write vaguely, so that there is little of substance to be disclosed
Write on personal devices, which are outside the Act
Say less in writing and more by phone, to avoid creating a record
Write records professionally and factually, knowing they might be disclosed

items.title: L9: Impartiality versus responsiveness
items.source: Civil Service Code; Cabinet Manual, chapter on general elections; Code of Conduct for Special Advisers
items.body: Civil servants must be both impartial and responsive. Impartial means they serve the government of the day without favouring any party. Responsive means they work effectively for ministers and carry out their policies, whether or not they agree with them. These duties can pull in different directions. A minister may ask for something that favours the governing party in subtle ways, for example a document that describes the government's record in unusually partisan language, or an event arranged in a way that serves a party's campaign. Officials must judge whether the request is for legitimate government purposes, which they should support, or party purposes, which they must not. A helpful test is whether the material would be proper if the other party were in power: government communications that explain, inform and justify policy are proper; those that attack opponents or promote a party are not. Where the request blends both purposes, officials can often do the legitimate part and decline the rest, explaining why, ideally through the private office or a senior official rather than through confrontation. Responsiveness also means being willing to implement a manifesto commitment even if officials have doubts; the electorate chose it. But officials should still give honest advice on delivery and cost. Special advisers are there to handle party political aspects, which offers a route: a minister who wants political material can ask their special adviser, who may use the party resources. At election time, the balance shifts toward caution. The permanent secretary and Cabinet Secretary guide officials in difficult cases. Officials who fear that impartiality is being compromised can use the Code's procedures to raise it, and the Commission is available as a last resort.

questions.prompt: A minister asks officials to write a government report in strongly partisan language. What is the best response?

options.text: Write it as asked, because the minister is entitled to set the tone of departmental documents
Write it but mark it as a draft to be checked later
Offer an objective, explanatory version and say why partisan wording is not appropriate
Write it but ask a special adviser to sign it off

questions.hint: Government documents should explain, not promote a party.

questions.prompt: What is a useful test for whether a request is proper?

options.text: Is the request from a minister, who is entitled to give instructions?
Would it be proper if the other party were in office?
Is it quick to deliver within the timetable set?
Is it popular with the public and the media?

questions.hint: The symmetrical test checks for party bias.

questions.prompt: A manifesto commitment is disliked by officials. How should they respond?

options.text: Slow it down until ministers drop it, since officials know it will not work
Refuse to work on it, since the policy has not been tested
Brief the opposition on its weaknesses so Parliament can scrutinise it
Implement it, giving honest advice on cost and delivery

questions.prompt: A request blends legitimate government communications with party promotion. What is often the best approach?

options.text: Do the legitimate part and decline the rest, explaining why
Decline the whole request, because it contains a party-political element
Do it all and register concerns afterwards
Pass the request to the opposition for their comment

questions.prompt: Where can a minister legitimately get party political material prepared?

options.text: From the policy team in the department, as part of the normal policy work
From the press office, using the department's communications budget
From the Government Communication Service, as part of a campaign
From their special adviser, using party resources

questions.prompt: Why does the balance shift toward caution at election time?

options.text: Because ministers are away campaigning and are less available to take decisions
Because the Cabinet Secretary temporarily takes over the minister's role
Officials must avoid actions that could influence the outcome or commit a future government
Because the Civil Service Code is suspended while the campaign is under way

questions.prompt: An official feels impartiality is being compromised by repeated requests. What is the sensible first step?

options.text: Raise it through their management chain, then the Code's procedures if needed
Go to the press, so the public hears about the pressure being put on officials
Stop working with the minister and ask for a move to another department
Write to the leader of the opposition, so Parliament can scrutinise the requests

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes responsiveness?

options.text: Doing whatever a minister asks, including anything that conflicts with the law or the Code
Working effectively for ministers and carrying out their policies, whatever officials think
Supporting the governing party's electoral prospects in the run-up to an election
Adjusting the advice officials give so that it suits the minister's known preference

questions.hint: Responsiveness is within the law and Code.

items.title: L9: Speed versus process in an emergency
items.source: Procurement Act 2023; Managing Public Money; National Audit Office reports on emergency procurement
items.body: In a crisis, such as a pandemic, flood or sudden supply failure, government must act fast, and normal processes can seem too slow. The rules allow flexibility: procurement law permits direct awards without competition where there is genuine urgency that could not have been foreseen, and the Treasury can agree faster approvals for spending. But urgency does not remove the need for propriety and regularity. Officials should still record why the decision was made, what alternatives were considered, who authorised it, how conflicts of interest were managed, and how value for money was judged. After the event, decisions will be examined by the National Audit Office, select committees and sometimes the courts. Past experience shows that quick decisions without a record, without checking suppliers' backgrounds, or with poor handling of conflicts can lead to waste, fraud and loss of public trust. A common mistake is to treat the emergency as a reason to skip documentation; another is to extend the emergency approach long after the crisis passes. Officials need to balance speed and control: simplified approvals can reduce time, but key checks, such as due diligence on suppliers and conflict declarations, should remain. Accounting officers can ask for a ministerial direction if they have concerns. Departments should plan for emergencies in advance, with frameworks, standing agreements and clear delegations, so that they do not need to cut corners. Transparency matters as well: contracts awarded without competition should be published promptly so that others can scrutinise them. Where a rule cannot be followed, the departure should be recorded, justified and, where required, reported to the Treasury.

questions.prompt: During an emergency, a manager wants to award a large contract to a supplier recommended by a minister's office with no record of the reasons. What is the main problem?

options.text: None, because an emergency removes the need to record the reasons for decisions
The supplier is not British, which makes it ineligible to receive the contract
Ministers cannot recommend suppliers to their department under any circumstances
Urgency allows speed, but reasons, conflict checks and value for money must still be recorded

questions.prompt: Which situation best justifies a direct award without competition?

options.text: Genuine urgency which could not have been foreseen
A supplier the department has used before and trusts
A wish to avoid the time and effort of a tender
A preference for a local supplier over a distant one

questions.hint: Urgency must be genuine and not self-created.

questions.prompt: Which checks should remain even in an emergency?

options.text: Competitive tendering in every case, however urgent
Parliament's approval of each contract before it is signed
Due diligence on suppliers and conflict declarations
A public consultation on the supplier chosen

questions.prompt: What does the National Audit Office do after an emergency?

options.text: Approves emergency contracts in advance so that waste is prevented
Examines whether decisions were properly made and value for money was achieved
Sets the department's emergency budget for the financial year in question
Appoints the suppliers that the department is then required to use

questions.hint: The NAO audits after the event.

questions.prompt: Why should contracts awarded without competition be published promptly?

options.text: So that others can scrutinise them
Because suppliers must give permission for publication
So that the department can avoid complaints from competitors
To satisfy the Speaker's request for contract details

questions.hint: Transparency compensates for lack of competition.

questions.prompt: A team continues using emergency procurement rules six months after the crisis ended. What is the issue?

options.text: None, as emergency rules last a year by default
The emergency rules are better than the normal ones, so should continue
It saves money, which is the main aim of procurement
The emergency approach should end when the urgency passes

questions.hint: Emergency flexibility should not become routine.

questions.prompt: What is the best way to reduce the need to cut corners in future emergencies?

options.text: Keep a large cash reserve, so that no approval is needed once an emergency begins
Ban ministers from taking any part in procurement decisions of any kind
Plan ahead with frameworks, standing agreements and clear delegations
Rely on volunteers and donated goods whenever an emergency arises

questions.prompt: If a rule cannot be followed in an emergency, what should be done?

options.text: Ignore the rule quietly and keep going, since time is short
Record the departure, justify it and report it where required
Ask the supplier to waive the requirement in its own contract
Wait for Parliament to approve the departure some time after the event

questions.hint: Departures must be recorded and justified.

items.title: L9: Propriety beyond legality
items.source: Managing Public Money, Annex 2.4; Nolan Principles; Civil Service Code
items.body: Something can be legal and still be improper. The accounting officer's tests treat regularity and propriety separately. Regularity asks whether spending has the proper legal authority. Propriety asks whether it meets the standards of public conduct, including fairness, honesty and avoiding conflicts of interest, and whether it would stand up to public scrutiny. For example, a department may have the legal power to pay a large sum to a consultant, but if the supplier was chosen because a minister's friend runs the company, or the reasons are not recorded, it may fail the propriety test. Similarly, a generous severance payment may fall within the rules but cause concern if the circumstances are questionable. Propriety also covers expenses, hospitality, and the use of public assets. A useful approach is to ask: would this be defensible if reported in the press, explained to Parliament, and judged by someone who disagreed with the policy? Does it reflect the Nolan Principles of selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness, honesty and leadership? Officials should be wary of the argument that because no rule is broken, there is no problem. Where there is doubt, they should seek advice from finance, legal and propriety teams, and escalate to the accounting officer. They should keep a record of their reasoning. Propriety is also about perceptions: a fair decision that looks unfair may still damage trust. Officials are expected to raise concerns, even where the action is lawful, and the accounting officer can ask for a ministerial direction on propriety grounds. Public bodies carry responsibility for stewardship of public money on behalf of taxpayers.

questions.prompt: A department has the legal power to award a grant, but the recipient is run by a friend of the minister and the selection process was not recorded. Which standard is most at risk?

options.text: Propriety
Regularity
Feasibility
Legality

questions.hint: Legal power does not settle propriety.

questions.prompt: Which question helps to test propriety?

options.text: Is it cheaper than the equivalent spending last year was?
Has the minister personally approved it in writing?
Would this stand up if reported in the press and explained to Parliament?
Is it within the budget allocated to the team for the year?

questions.prompt: An official says no rule has been broken, so there is no issue. What is the best reply?

options.text: Agree, because rules set the whole standard of conduct
Propriety goes beyond rules to whether conduct meets public standards
Ask the minister whether they would like to check it
Say the rules are out of date and need to be changed

questions.hint: Rules do not exhaust the standards.

questions.prompt: Which of the Nolan Principles is most directly engaged by choosing a supplier because of friendship?

options.text: Leadership
Openness
Accountability
Objectivity

questions.prompt: A decision is fair but looks unfair to the public. Why might it still matter?

options.text: Perceptions do not matter if the decision was fair
Appearances matter only to the press, not to the public
Perceptions affect public trust
The law requires every decision to look fair

questions.prompt: If an official doubts the propriety of a payment, what should they do?

options.text: Pay it now and check the propriety afterwards, so the supplier is not left waiting
Seek advice from finance, legal or propriety colleagues, then escalate to the accounting officer
Ask the supplier whether it considers the payment to be acceptable
Delay it indefinitely without telling anyone why it has not been paid

questions.prompt: On what grounds can an accounting officer request a ministerial direction?

options.text: Any political disagreement between ministers and the officials who advise them
Only legal concerns about whether the policy is lawful
Only cost overruns above a set level agreed with the Treasury
Regularity, propriety, value for money or feasibility concerns

questions.prompt: Which of these falls within propriety rather than regularity?

options.text: Whether hospitality offered to staff could appear to influence them
Whether Parliament voted the money in the Estimates
Whether a statutory instrument was laid correctly
Whether the Treasury approved the budget line

items.title: L9: National consistency versus local discretion
items.source: Cabinet Office, delivery guidance; Equality Act 2010; Public Sector Equality Duty
items.body: Public services face a recurring tension between consistent national standards and local flexibility. Consistency promotes fairness: people in similar circumstances should receive similar treatment, wherever they live or whichever official handles their case. It also makes services easier to understand and audit. Local discretion allows services to reflect local needs, use professional judgement and be more responsive, for example in how a local jobcentre helps a particular claimant. Too little discretion produces rigid decisions that fail people in unusual circumstances; too much produces variation that looks arbitrary and may be discriminatory, sometimes called a postcode lottery. Policy designers use guidance, decision-making frameworks, training and quality assurance to manage the balance. Law may set eligibility rules, with discretion limited to how they are applied, such as awarding a hardship payment. Decision-makers must act within their powers, take account of relevant considerations, ignore irrelevant ones, and give reasons. Decisions can be challenged by internal review, tribunal appeal or judicial review. Devolution adds another layer: different nations may legitimately make different choices on devolved matters, which is a deliberate use of difference rather than inconsistency. For officials, good practice is to apply the rules consistently, use discretion where it is intended and record the reasons, and to flag patterns of unexplained variation so that policy teams can review. Monitoring data by region, team or protected characteristic can reveal unfairness. Local innovation can be valuable if it is tested and shared, but it should not undermine legal duties. Where discretion is used to benefit one person, officials should ask whether they would do the same for anyone in the same situation.

questions.prompt: Two jobcentres in different regions treat similar claimants very differently, with no stated reason. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: It is proof that local discretion is working exactly as the policy intended
It may indicate unexplained variation that should be flagged and reviewed
It is a legal requirement of devolution, which allows regions to differ
It is a matter for local staff and managers to deal with, not policy teams

questions.prompt: Policy gives a decision-maker discretion to award a hardship payment. What must they still do?

options.text: Follow their instincts, since discretion means freedom to decide as they see fit
Choose whichever customer presents their case most persuasively
Act within their powers, weigh relevant factors, ignore irrelevant ones and give reasons
Apply a flat rate to everyone, whatever their individual circumstances

questions.prompt: The Welsh Government and UK Government make different decisions on a devolved matter. How should this be seen?

options.text: As a breach of national standards that the UK Government must correct
As evidence that one government has made an error
As a breach of the Civil Service Code by devolved officials
As a legitimate result of devolution, not inconsistency

questions.prompt: Which approach best manages the balance between consistency and discretion?

options.text: Guidance, training, quality assurance and monitoring, with reasons recorded
Strict rules with no exceptions allowed, so the same decision is reached in every case
Complete discretion for each decision-maker with no rules, to allow flexibility
Annual reviews of policy only, without monitoring outcomes in between

questions.prompt: An official wants to use discretion to help one customer with a sympathetic story. What question is useful?

options.text: Will the customer be grateful for my help in this case?
Will my manager notice what I have done, and approve of it?
Is the customer polite and cooperative enough to deserve help?
Would I do the same for anyone in the same situation?

questions.prompt: Monitoring outcomes by protected characteristic shows one group is refused far more often. What does the public sector equality duty suggest?

options.text: Investigate the cause and consider whether practice needs to change
Ignore it, because the rules were followed in every case
Stop monitoring by characteristic, since it raises awkward questions
Publish the figures without comment and without any review

questions.prompt: What is the main risk of too little discretion?

options.text: Excessive variation between regions that looks arbitrary to the public
Rigid decisions that fail people in unusual circumstances
Weak audit trails, because decisions are taken without any recorded reasons
Higher spending on staff, as every decision needs a manager to review it

questions.prompt: Local innovation is proposed. Which condition makes it safer?

options.text: It is kept private, to avoid copying by others
It is introduced across the country at once, to save time
It is tested, evaluated and shared and does not undermine legal duties
It avoids collecting data, which would slow it down

items.title: L9: Independence of arm's length bodies
items.source: Cabinet Office, Public Bodies Reform and Classification guidance; Regulators' Code; Legislation Act-specific statutes
items.body: Some bodies are placed at arm's length from ministers because their work needs independence. The Cabinet Office's review of public bodies in 2010 suggested three tests for a body to exist outside a department: that it performs a technical function that needs external expertise, that its activity needs political impartiality, or that it needs to act independently to establish facts. Regulators, tribunals, some advisory bodies, and statistical authorities fit these tests. Independence is not total. Ministers appoint chairs and boards, set the legal framework, provide funding, and are accountable to Parliament for the system as a whole. But in individual decisions, such as a regulator deciding on a licence or the Office for National Statistics publishing a statistic, ministers must not interfere. Some independence is set in statute, and a minister who tries to direct a body outside their legal powers risks judicial review. Funding can be used as an informal pressure point, and this is one reason that financial independence is sometimes protected. Boards are accountable for the body's performance and independent decisions, and the chief executive is accountable as accounting officer. Sponsor departments should keep a sound relationship: they can ask questions, request information and discuss priorities, but must not seek to influence individual decisions. If something goes wrong, the minister has to explain, without having directed the decision. A dilemma arises when a body's decision is controversial and the minister is under political pressure to intervene. Officials should advise ministers on what the law allows, the risk to the body's independence and public trust, and the options within the minister's powers, such as changing guidance or legislating for the future.

questions.prompt: A minister under pressure from the press asks officials how to overturn an independent regulator's decision on a specific licence. What advice is proper?

options.text: Show how to pressure the regulator informally, which avoids a formal instruction
Explain that individual decisions are the regulator's, and set out options such as changing the framework
Provide a draft instruction to the regulator that overrides its decision on the licence
Recommend withdrawing the regulator's funding until it changes its decision

questions.prompt: Which of the tests is used to justify a body at arm's length?

options.text: Its activity needs political impartiality
It is cheaper to run than a department
It employs more staff than a department could
It reports directly to the Prime Minister

questions.hint: One of three tests is impartiality.

questions.prompt: Which action is a proper use of a sponsor department's relationship?

options.text: Reviewing each decision before it is made, to make sure the body gets it right
Sending departmental staff to sit on the body's decision panels
Approving each licence before the regulator is allowed to issue it
Asking questions and discussing priorities without influencing individual decisions

questions.prompt: Why might funding be seen as a risk to independence?

options.text: It is always paid late, which weakens the body
It is never transparent, so cannot be monitored
It can be used informally as pressure
It cannot be measured, so is hard to protect

questions.prompt: A statistical authority publishes a figure which embarrasses ministers. What follows?

options.text: Ministers can delay publication until the policy is announced
Ministers can require changes to the figures before publication
The Cabinet Secretary must approve the release
Ministers can explain and respond, but must not interfere with the publication

questions.prompt: Who is accountable for the body's independent decisions?

options.text: The sponsor minister alone, as the body is funded through their department
Its board and chief executive
The Prime Minister, as the minister responsible for the Civil Service
The Treasury, which provides the body's funding and sets its limits

questions.prompt: What can a minister do about a controversial decision they cannot lawfully direct?

options.text: Reverse it by a ministerial statement, since the minister is accountable for the body
Remove the board immediately and appoint one that will decide differently
Explain it and consider whether the framework or guidance should change in future
Ask Parliament to annul the decision by a vote in the Commons

questions.prompt: What risk does a minister face if they direct a body beyond their legal powers?

options.text: Judicial review
A vote of no confidence
A Treasury penalty
Dismissal by the board

items.title: L9: Duty to the employer versus duty to the public
items.source: Civil Service Code; Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998; Official Secrets Act 1989
items.body: Civil servants owe loyalty to their ministers and department, but also duties to Parliament, the law and the public interest. Usually these align. Sometimes they conflict, for example when an official believes that a decision is hiding serious risk to the public, or that Parliament has been misled. The Code reflects this by saying that civil servants must not misuse their position, must not disclose official information without authority, and must also report improper conduct. It provides a ladder of responses. First, raise the concern with the line manager or other senior official. If unresolved, use the nominated officer or whistleblowing route. If still unresolved, bring it to the Civil Service Commission. Only in limited circumstances would going outside this route be justifiable, and then legal advice is important because disclosure of classified material may be a criminal offence under the Official Secrets Act, and the Public Interest Disclosure Act protects only some disclosures. The public interest is not simply what an individual thinks is right: officials are expected to weigh the likelihood and seriousness of harm, the evidence they have, whether the concern could be resolved internally, and whether disclosure would cause its own harm. Acting in haste, on rumour, or from personal grievance undermines credibility. Careful records of what was raised, with whom and when, support any later explanation. An official who raises concerns properly should not suffer detriment, and managers have a duty to take concerns seriously and protect those who raise them. A culture where people feel they can speak up reduces the chance that anyone feels forced to consider going outside. The balance between loyalty and public duty is a matter of judgement, and the Code gives guidance without removing the need for care.

questions.prompt: An official believes a decision conceals a serious safety risk to the public. What is the most appropriate first step?

options.text: Contact a journalist, so that the public can hear about the risk as quickly as possible
Raise it with their line manager or another senior official and record that they did
Contact the opposition, who can raise the matter in Parliament without delay
Post about it on social media, to gather support from colleagues and the public

questions.prompt: After raising a concern internally, the official feels nothing has been done. What comes next in the Code's ladder?

options.text: Use the nominated officer or whistleblowing route, then the Civil Service Commission
Go public immediately, because the internal route has failed to act
Resign and make a public statement about the concern
Wait six months and raise it again with the same manager

questions.prompt: Why is legal advice important before disclosing classified material externally?

options.text: It is always protected under the Public Interest Disclosure Act, whatever it contains
The Civil Service Code forbids officials from taking legal advice about disclosures
The Civil Service Commission requires legal advice before any disclosure is made
It may be an offence under the Official Secrets Act and protections may not apply

questions.prompt: Which factor best shows careful judgement of the public interest?

options.text: The strength of the individual's feelings about the issue and their sense of duty
The popularity of the cause with the public and the press
Weighing how serious and likely the harm is, and whether it can be resolved internally
How much publicity the disclosure is likely to attract for the cause

questions.prompt: Which behaviour undermines the credibility of a concern?

options.text: Acting on rumour or personal grievance without evidence
Keeping notes of what was raised, with whom and when
Raising the concern as soon as it is noticed
Seeking confidential advice before acting on the concern

questions.prompt: What should a manager do when told of a concern?

options.text: Ask who else knows, so that the circle of people aware can be kept small
Take it seriously, protect the person and ensure it is looked into
Tell the colleague concerned straight away, so they can respond
Dismiss it for now if the person has no proof yet

questions.hint: Managers must protect those who raise concerns.

questions.prompt: How does a culture of speaking up help?

options.text: It guarantees that no concerns ever arise
It makes leaks lawful
It reduces the chance that anyone feels forced to go outside
It replaces the Civil Service Code

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the Code's position on loyalty and public duty?

options.text: Loyalty to ministers outranks every other duty of a civil servant
Duty to the public always outweighs the duty of confidentiality
The two duties never conflict in practice, so judgement is not needed
Loyalty to ministers is real, but sits within duties to the law, Parliament and honesty

items.title: L9: Evidence and uncertainty in advice
items.source: Civil Service Code; Government Chief Scientific Adviser guidance; Government Social Research Code; The Aqua Book
items.body: Ministers rely on officials and analysts for evidence, but evidence is often incomplete or uncertain. Good advice states what is known, what is not known, how confident the analysts are and how the answer might change with new evidence. Analysts follow professional codes: economists, statisticians, social researchers and scientists must be objective and honest about limitations. The Aqua Book sets standards for quality assurance of analysis, including proportionate checks, clear ownership and independent review of important models. The Civil Service Code's objectivity value requires officials not to ignore inconvenient facts. A common problem is pressure for a single number or a firm conclusion where the evidence supports only a range. Presenting false precision may mislead; offering a range with an explanation of assumptions is more honest and more useful. Another problem is selective use of evidence, called cherry-picking, to support a preferred view. Officials should be transparent about how evidence was gathered and which sources were not available. Where evidence conflicts, the advice should explain the reasons, and where judgement is needed, say whose judgement and why. Publishing analysis, subject to security and commercial confidentiality, supports public trust, and analysts should be able to correct errors openly. Ministers may legitimately weigh values and political considerations alongside evidence, but officials should make clear which parts of the advice are factual and which are judgement. When ministers publicly use evidence in a way that overstates it, the statistics regulator, the Office for Statistics Regulation, can intervene on official statistics, and officials should consider whether to draw it to ministers' attention. Officials should avoid the opposite error as well: using uncertainty as an excuse to avoid advising.

questions.prompt: A minister asks for a single figure for the cost of a policy, but analysts can only support a range. What is the best response?

options.text: Give the mid-point of the range and present it as the expected cost without caveats
Give the lowest figure in the range, as it is the one the analysts judge most helpful
Give the range and explain the assumptions that most affect where the true figure falls
Hold back any figure until further research has narrowed the uncertainty to a single value

questions.prompt: What is meant by cherry-picking evidence?

options.text: Selecting the cheapest source of data for an analysis to keep research costs down
Choosing which staff should work on an analytical project based on their seniority
Publishing every available dataset, whether or not it is relevant to the question
Choosing only the findings that support a view already held, and leaving out the rest

questions.prompt: What is the Aqua Book about?

options.text: Standards for quality assurance of analysis, including important models, used in government
Rules for procuring goods and services through frameworks and standing contracts
Guidance on how parliamentary Bills should be drafted and introduced
Standards for how government communications campaigns should be planned

questions.hint: The Aqua Book concerns analytical quality.

questions.prompt: Two studies reach conflicting results on the same policy. How should advice to ministers handle this?

options.text: Present only the study that fits the policy and mention the other briefly in an annex
Explain the conflict and its likely causes, and say which judgement the advice rests on
Average the two results and present the average as the finding, to avoid confusion
Leave out both studies, since conflicting evidence cannot support any recommendation

questions.hint: Transparency about conflicts keeps advice honest.

questions.prompt: A minister uses a statistic in a speech in a way that overstates what it shows. What might officials properly do?

options.text: Draw it to the minister's attention and consider whether a correction is needed
Take no action, because the statistic itself is real and the minister's wording is political
Contact the press office to issue a correction without telling the minister
Ask the minister's opponents to challenge the claim publicly in Parliament

questions.hint: The Code requires honest use of evidence.

questions.prompt: Why should advice make clear which parts are fact and which are judgement?

options.text: So that officials can avoid responsibility for the judgements they have made
So that the minister can see where evidence ends and views begin before deciding
So that the advice appears longer and more thorough to the decision-maker
So that departmental lawyers can approve each part of the advice separately

questions.hint: Clarity helps ministers weigh the advice.

questions.prompt: Which is the opposite error to false precision in analysis?

options.text: Giving a range of figures with the assumptions explained clearly
Publishing the assumptions on which a model rests
Asking for an independent review of an important model
Using uncertainty as an excuse for not giving any advice at all

questions.hint: Uncertain evidence still needs a recommendation.

questions.prompt: Why does publishing analysis, where security and commercial confidentiality allow, help the Civil Service?

options.text: It raises the cost of research, which deters weak proposals
It prevents criticism, because the work has already been seen
Others can scrutinise it and errors can be found and corrected openly
It speeds up decisions by removing the need for ministerial approval

questions.hint: Open analysis supports trust and quality.

items.title: L9: Short-term delivery versus long-term capability
items.source: National Audit Office, Lessons learned reports; Government Functional Standards; Spending Review guidance
items.body: Departments face pressure to deliver visible results quickly, often within the lifetime of a Parliament or a ministerial term. But some of the best public value comes from long-term investment in skills, systems and prevention, whose benefits show later. This creates a trade-off. Annual budgets and short political horizons can push departments to defer maintenance, delay upgrading ageing IT, or cut training. The National Audit Office has repeatedly noted that legacy systems and reduced capability increase risk and cost over time. Ministers and the Treasury make the final decisions, but officials should present the long-term consequences honestly, using techniques such as whole-life costing, scenario planning and risk assessments. Prevention is a case in point: early intervention in health, housing or justice can save money later but the benefit accrues elsewhere or after the minister has moved on, which makes it hard to prioritise. Spending Reviews set multi-year budgets to give some certainty. Departments can also protect long-term capability by keeping a pipeline of skills, planning workforce needs and building knowledge management so that experience is not lost when people move on, as frequent job moves can weaken delivery of long projects. Major projects should have senior responsible owners who stay in post long enough to see progress, and clear benefit tracking. Officials should also be careful about optimism bias, which leads to underestimating the cost and time of long programmes. Where there is a conflict between short-term savings and long-term resilience, advice should set out the trade-off plainly and, if relevant, the risk transferred to future years. Short-term gains that create hidden liabilities are not value for money.

questions.prompt: A department proposes to postpone replacing an ageing IT system to meet this year's savings target. What should advice to the minister include?

options.text: Only the saving, since the target set by the Treasury is the objective
The saving, the growing risk and whole-life cost of delay, and a clear recommendation
A note that IT replacement is an operational matter and not for ministers
A proposal to cut training budgets instead, without setting out the effects

questions.hint: Trade-offs should be set out honestly.

questions.prompt: Why is prevention hard to prioritise in spending decisions?

options.text: Prevention has been shown never to work in public services
Prevention always costs more than responding to a problem later
The benefits may come later or accrue to other departments or other ministers
Prevention cannot be measured, so Treasury rules do not allow funding it

questions.hint: Delayed and dispersed benefits weaken the case.

questions.prompt: What does whole-life costing look at?

options.text: Only the running costs once the asset has been bought and installed
Only the purchase price, since later costs are uncertain and difficult to forecast
The costs to one department, ignoring costs that fall on others
The costs over the full life of an asset or service, not just the initial price

questions.hint: Whole-life costs show the true price.

questions.prompt: How can frequent job moves weaken the delivery of long projects?

options.text: Knowledge, relationships and ownership are lost each time a key person leaves
People work harder during the first months of a new job, which distorts the plan
Projects speed up when new staff arrive, but then lose direction
Moves affect pay but have no effect on how a project is delivered

questions.prompt: Why does the Spending Review set budgets over several years?

options.text: To reduce the Treasury's workload by holding fewer annual negotiations
To let departments overspend one year and make up for it in the next
To avoid Parliament having to approve Estimates each year
To give departments some certainty for planning beyond a single year

questions.prompt: Which arrangement best supports accountability on a major project?

options.text: A senior responsible owner who stays in post long enough to see progress and benefits
A new owner every six months, to bring fresh challenge to the project
A committee of equals, with no single named person accountable
Oversight by the Treasury alone, without an owner in the delivering department

questions.prompt: What effect does optimism bias have on a long programme?

options.text: Costs are overestimated, so projects are never started
Benefits are underestimated, so good projects are rejected
Costs and timescales are underestimated and benefits overstated
Risks are overestimated, which makes teams too cautious

questions.prompt: How should a short-term saving that creates hidden future liabilities be judged?

options.text: As sensible, since a saving this year is certain and future costs are not
As poor value for money, because the costs have only moved to later years
As required by law, whenever the Treasury sets a savings target
As an improvement in propriety, because public money is being protected

items.title: L9: Competing demands from several governments
items.source: Cabinet Office, Intergovernmental relations guidance; Devolution guidance notes; Common frameworks
items.body: Officials in UK departments sometimes face competing demands from several governments at once. A UK-wide policy may touch devolved areas, so the Scottish, Welsh and Northern Ireland governments may have different priorities, different political parties in office and different legal powers. The UK Government may want a single approach for efficiency, a market that works across the UK or international commitments, while devolved governments want to use their powers to pursue different policies. Civil servants in each government serve their own ministers and cannot speak for another government, but must work constructively across boundaries. Good practice includes early engagement, sharing drafts of relevant material under agreed confidentiality, clear points of contact, and escalating disagreements through official-level and ministerial forums set up under intergovernmental agreements. Disputes can be referred through a defined process and ultimately may be decided by ministers or, in legal cases, by the courts. Officials should avoid surprising other governments, for example by announcing something in a devolved area without notice. They also need to avoid giving commitments for which they lack authority, and to be clear about what is agreed and what remains open. Financial issues, such as how changes to UK spending affect devolved budgets through the Barnett formula, may be a source of tension, and the Treasury is involved. The Home Civil Service shares a Code, and civil servants in the devolved administrations are part of it, but they serve devolved ministers. Because the governments may be of different parties, impartiality is again important: officials must not use information from one government to disadvantage another for party reasons. Joint working must also preserve each government's confidential information, because trust underpins collaboration.

questions.prompt: A UK department plans an announcement affecting a devolved matter. What does good practice suggest?

options.text: Announce it first and brief the devolved governments afterwards so the news is not leaked
Seek the views of the opposition parties in each nation before announcing it
Give the devolved governments early notice and be clear what is agreed and what is open
Delay it until all four governments have formally agreed to the wording

questions.prompt: A devolved government official asks a UK official to commit the UK Government to extra funding. What is the right approach?

options.text: Agree in principle to maintain goodwill, and sort out the detail later
Refer the request to Parliament, which holds the power over funding
Decline to discuss funding with another government at all
Make clear they lack authority to commit, and pass the request to those who have it

questions.hint: Do not commit beyond your authority.

questions.prompt: How are disagreements between governments usually handled?

options.text: They are decided by the Civil Service Commission on each side's evidence
They are escalated through official-level and ministerial forums set by intergovernmental arrangements
They are decided by the Speaker, as the neutral officer of Parliament
They are left unresolved until the next election changes one of the governments

questions.prompt: A devolved civil servant learns confidential UK Government plans in joint work. How should they treat them?

options.text: Keep them confidential and not use them to disadvantage the UK Government for party reasons
Pass them to devolved ministers, who are entitled to know what the UK is planning
Publish them if the plans affect the people of their nation
Share them with the press to put pressure on the UK Government

questions.prompt: For whom does a Scottish Government civil servant work?

options.text: UK ministers, since they are in the Home Civil Service
Scottish ministers, while bound by the Civil Service Code
The Cabinet Secretary, who directs all civil servants in the UK
The presiding officer of the Scottish Parliament

questions.prompt: Which issue often causes financial tension between governments?

options.text: How changes in UK spending feed through to devolved budgets by the Barnett formula
The dates on which each parliament goes into recess each year
The branding used on GOV.UK pages in each nation
The cost of overseas travel by ministers from each government

questions.hint: Funding formulas matter to devolved budgets.

questions.prompt: Why might the UK Government want one approach across the whole UK in some areas?

options.text: To make devolution less meaningful in the areas concerned
To increase the number of civil servants in London
For efficiency, a functioning UK-wide market or international commitments
To reduce scrutiny from the devolved parliaments

questions.prompt: What does impartiality require when the governments are of different parties?

options.text: Supporting whichever party leads the government that employs the official
Staying silent in joint meetings, to avoid taking sides
Sharing all papers with every government, whatever their confidentiality
Not using information from one government to disadvantage another for party reasons

items.title: L9: Loyalty to colleagues and the Code
items.source: Civil Service Code; ACAS guidance on workplace conduct; departmental conduct policies
items.body: Working relationships are built on trust, and most civil servants want to support their colleagues. Difficult situations arise when loyalty to a colleague collides with the Code. A colleague may make an error, cut a corner, claim an expense they should not, or behave badly to others. Covering for them, for example by not mentioning a mistake that affects customers, can seem kind but may breach the honesty and integrity values and cause greater harm later. The Code asks civil servants to report breaches and to be honest about mistakes. The sensible response is proportionate. For a minor error that is quickly corrected and does not harm anyone, a quiet word with the colleague and encouragement to tell the manager may be enough. For something that affects customers or public money, or that is deliberate, it should be reported, even if uncomfortable. Where bullying or harassment is involved, the department's policies and the duty of care to colleagues apply, and managers have a duty to act. Supporting a colleague can mean helping them to put things right, suggesting they speak to their manager, and offering to go with them, rather than concealing the problem. If a colleague asks you to keep a secret that involves wrongdoing, you cannot promise that. Being honest about your own role matters too: if you were part of the error, say so. A team culture that treats mistakes as learning opportunities makes honest reporting easier. Managers should respond fairly, so that people are not punished for reporting. Where there is a real conflict, officials can seek confidential advice from the nominated officer or HR before deciding what to do.

questions.prompt: A colleague tells you they made an error that overpaid a customer and asks you to tell nobody. What is the best response?

options.text: Keep the secret, because loyalty to a colleague comes before the department
Tell the customer yourself so the money is repaid quickly
Correct the error on the system yourself without telling anyone
Say you cannot keep it quiet, encourage them to tell the manager and offer to help

questions.hint: You cannot promise secrecy about wrongdoing.

questions.prompt: Which response suits a minor error that was quickly corrected with no harm to anyone?

options.text: A quiet word and encouragement to mention it to the manager
A formal complaint through the department's grievance process
A report to the Civil Service Commission
A note to the press office in case it becomes known

questions.prompt: A colleague deliberately claims an expense they know is not allowed. What should you do?

options.text: Ignore it, since the sum involved is small
Report it through the proper route, even though it is uncomfortable
Confront them in front of the team
Submit a similar claim to show it is accepted practice

questions.hint: Deliberate misuse of public money is serious.

questions.prompt: A team makes an error and you were part of it. What does honesty require?

options.text: Say nothing unless someone asks you directly
Blame the system so that no individual is singled out
Say so, including your own part, when the error is discussed
Wait for someone else to mention it first

questions.prompt: A colleague is bullying a junior team member. Who has a duty to act?

options.text: Only the junior member, who must make a formal complaint
Nobody, unless the department has first received a formal complaint
Only the Civil Service Commission
Managers, under the department's policies and duty of care

questions.hint: Managers owe a duty of care.

questions.prompt: Which team culture makes honest reporting easier?

options.text: One that rewards people who never report errors, so that few are recorded
One that treats mistakes as chances to learn, without blaming those who report
One that punishes every mistake severely, to deter others from making them
One that keeps problems within the team so that the department's image is protected

questions.prompt: Who can give confidential advice if you are unsure what to do about a colleague's conduct?

options.text: The nominated officer or HR
The press office
A friend in another department
A trade union representative only

questions.prompt: Why can covering for a colleague cause greater harm than reporting?

options.text: It makes the colleague more dependent on you and strains the working relationship
It may delay delivery of the team's work while the problem is hidden
The problem can grow, affect customers and leave you party to a breach of honesty
It has no consequences for anyone so long as the error is never discovered

items.title: L9: Correcting the record
items.source: Ministerial Code, para 1.3; Civil Service Code; House of Commons Procedure
items.body: A basic constitutional duty is that Parliament must be given accurate information. The Ministerial Code says that ministers who knowingly mislead Parliament will be expected to offer their resignation, and that if an inadvertent error is made, the minister should correct the record at the earliest opportunity. Officials have a role in helping ministers to meet this duty. When drafting answers, briefing for debates or preparing statements, they should check the facts, avoid wording that creates a false impression, and flag uncertainty. If officials realise that something said to Parliament was inaccurate, they should tell the private office immediately, so that the minister can correct it by a written ministerial statement, a letter to the committee, or a correction in Hansard through the proper channel. Delay creates risk, because the longer an error stands, the more likely it is that others will rely on it, and that it will look like concealment. The Civil Service Code also requires officials not to deceive or knowingly mislead ministers, Parliament or others, and applies where officials give evidence themselves. The test is not only literal truth but whether the overall impression is true. A technically accurate statement that leaves a misleading impression is not acceptable. If a minister refuses to correct a significant error that officials know about, the matter should be raised with a senior official, and where necessary through the Code's procedures. Officials should keep a note of what was drawn to the minister's attention. A culture in which errors are reported without blame is essential. Corrections should be proportionate and clear: they should say what was wrong, what the correct information is, and, where relevant, what effect the error had. Late corrections should explain the reasons for delay. Correcting the record is not weakness; it shows respect for Parliament.

questions.prompt: Officials realise that a figure in the minister's statement to Parliament last week was wrong. What should they do first?

options.text: Tell the private office immediately so the minister can correct the record
Wait to see whether anyone notices before acting
Prepare a defence of the figure in case it is challenged
Brief a journalist so the correction comes from outside government

questions.prompt: What does the Ministerial Code expect when a minister has made an inadvertent error to Parliament?

options.text: Resign automatically, however minor the error
Leave it uncorrected unless an MP asks about it
Ask the Speaker to remove the statement from the record
Correct the record at the earliest opportunity

questions.prompt: A statement to Parliament is technically true but leaves a misleading overall impression. How does the Code treat it?

options.text: It is acceptable, since each word of the statement is literally true
It is not acceptable, because the overall impression must also be accurate
It is acceptable if a special adviser has approved the wording
It is acceptable if the same wording is repeated consistently afterwards

questions.prompt: Why is delay in correcting an error risky?

options.text: Corrections become more expensive to publish over time
The Speaker will fine the department for late corrections
Others may rely on it, and the delay can look like concealment
The minister loses the right to vote in the House

questions.prompt: A minister refuses to correct a significant error that officials know about. What might officials do?

options.text: Brief the press so that the error is corrected publicly
Send a correction to Parliament themselves in the minister's name
Raise it with a senior official and, if needed, use the Code's procedures
Resign from their post without raising the matter

questions.prompt: Which of these should a correction include?

options.text: What was wrong, what the correct information is and, where relevant, its effect
Only the corrected figure, without any explanation of the error
A defence of the original statement, to show it was reasonable
An apology to the Speaker, whatever the error was

questions.prompt: How might a minister correct an error made in the chamber?

options.text: By posting a correction on the department's social media account only
By issuing a press release to the media only, without telling Parliament
By telling a journalist, who will report the correction
By a written ministerial statement or another proper parliamentary channel

questions.prompt: Why does a no-blame culture for reporting errors matter?

options.text: It guarantees that no further errors will occur once people are not blamed
It makes it more likely that errors are reported early, so they can be corrected
It removes accountability from those who make errors in their work
It makes formal corrections to Parliament unnecessary in future
